passage:
Elif had not spoken to Rafael all morning, and the Porto flat felt smaller because of it. At lunch she finally set down her fork. "Three years we lived here. I covered your rent when you lost the café job. And now you just leave me for Berlin."
Rafael felt the familiar tug in his chest. He made himself ask the question slowly, in his head: did I actually wrong her? He had told her in March, two months early, as their flat agreement said. He had paid back the café months by summer. The answer was no.
"I'm grateful for that rent, truly," he said. "And I'm still going. I'll help you find someone good for my room, and I'll call on Sundays."
Elif's eyes filled. "It won't be the same."
"No," he said gently. "It won't. I'll miss this too."
That evening they wrote the room advert together, arguing over whether to mention the noisy tram.

qa.q: When had Rafael told Elif about moving?
qa.a: Rafael told her in March, two months early, as their flat agreement said.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when Elif mentioned the rent she had covered?
qa.a: He felt a familiar tug of guilt in his chest, pulled between gratitude and the urge to give in.

qa.q: What turning point let Rafael keep his decision?
qa.a: Slowly asking himself whether he had actually wronged Elif, and checking the facts, showed the answer was no, so he could stay kind without changing his plan.

qa.q: How does Elif experience Rafael's calm answer?
qa.a: She still feels sad that it won't be the same, but being thanked and helped with the room lets her grieve the change instead of fighting it.

grounding: A young man checks whether he really wronged Elif, finds he did not, and keeps his move abroad while showing care in words and practical help.

"Seriously, Baljeet? After I stayed till midnight for your audit in March?" Sunaina dropped the shift roster on his desk in the hospital billing office. "Everyone always leaves me holding everything."
Baljeet's first instinct was to say fine, he would work Saturday. Instead he pulled up the roster history on his screen. He had covered for Sunaina twice since March. Saturday was his sister's graduation, marked on the leave calendar six weeks ago.
But one thing was true. Last Friday he had left without handing over the insurance files, and Sunaina had spent her evening finding them.
"You're right about Friday," he said. "That was my mistake, and I'm sorry. It won't happen again. Saturday I can't do. I can take your Tuesday late shift instead, if that helps."
Sunaina folded her arms, then unfolded them. "Tuesday helps," she muttered.
He wrote a note in his planner: handover checklist, every Friday.

qa.q: Where does the scene take place?
qa.a: It takes place in the hospital billing office.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet check the roster history before answering?
qa.a: He felt the pull to give in and wanted to know whether he had really wronged Sunaina or was only being pressured.

qa.q: Which part of Baljeet's reply worked, and why?
qa.a: He apologised plainly for the real mistake on Friday but kept his Saturday leave and offered the Tuesday shift, which showed care without giving in to pressure.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when her Friday complaint is admitted?
qa.a: She likely feels heard and less alone, which is why her folded arms loosen and she accepts the Tuesday offer.

grounding: A young man separates one real lapse, which he apologises for, from pressure to give up his leave, and keeps his decision while offering care.

passage:
Subject: About Saturday

Dear Noor,
I've been thinking about your message since yesterday. You said you can't believe I'm not coming to your café launch, after all the times you helped me move flats, and that you guess you know who your real friends are.
It stung. So I did what I try to do when I feel guilty: I asked myself whether I actually did something wrong.
I told you three weeks ago that Saturday is my sister's engagement. You said then that it was fine. I haven't changed the plan. I don't think I've wronged you.
But I do care, a lot. You did help me move, twice, and I haven't forgotten. So I'll come by on Friday evening to help set up the tables, and I'll bring my cousins on Sunday as your first customers.
I'm still not coming on Saturday. I hope you understand. And I hope the launch is wonderful.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What is happening for Chaitanya's sister on Saturday?
qa.a: Saturday is Chaitanya's sister's engagement.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel reading Noor's message?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt stung and guilty, which led to asking whether anything wrong had actually been done.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya show care without giving in?
qa.a: By offering to help set up on Friday and bringing cousins on Sunday, while keeping the decision to miss Saturday.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this email?
qa.a: Noor may still feel disappointed, but also reassured that Chaitanya cares and remembers the help.

grounding: An adult asks whether a friend was actually wronged, finds not, and keeps the decision while showing care in words and action.

passage:
So, Disha, you asked how the call with my mother went. Honestly? Hard.
I told her I'd accepted the job in Bangalore. There was silence. Then she said, "Go. What do I matter? I raised you alone, and now I'll grow old alone." Then she hung up.
I sat there with this huge weight. For an hour I was ready to call back and say I'd stay.
Then I did the thing my counsellor taught me. I asked, "Did I actually wrong her?" I'm Chetan, I'm twenty-four, I found a good job, and I'll be a two-hour flight away. That's not a wrong. Her loneliness is real. My leaving isn't a crime.
So I called back. I said, "Ma, I love you. I'm still going. I'll call every Sunday, and I'll fly home for Diwali." She cried. I stayed calm. I didn't argue about who sacrificed what.
It still hurts. But I'm going.

qa.q: When did Chetan promise to call his mother?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after his mother hung up?
qa.a: Chetan felt a huge weight of guilt, almost ready to call back and stay.

qa.q: What helped Chetan separate real guilt from pressure?
qa.a: Asking whether any wrong had actually been done, then keeping the decision while offering care: Sunday calls and coming home for Diwali.

qa.q: How might Chetan's mother be feeling?
qa.a: Chetan's mother is probably lonely and scared of growing old alone, which is real, even if her words put pressure on Chetan.

grounding: An adult asks whether a mother was actually wronged, finds not, and keeps the decision to move while showing care.

I sit next to Noor at the pharmacy counter, so I heard Eshaan's request on Thursday.
"Noor, cover my Sunday shift. Come on. After all the times I've covered for you." He said it loudly, with a sigh, the way he always does.
Noor didn't answer straight away. I saw her open the roster on her phone and scroll. I don't know exactly what she was thinking, but she took her time.
Then she said, calmly, "You covered for me once, in March, and I covered for you twice after that. I'm not able to do this Sunday. I'm sorry you're stuck, and I hope you find someone. I can ask Priti for you."
Eshaan rolled his eyes. "Wow. Okay." Noor didn't argue.
Later I asked her if she felt bad. She said, "A bit. But feeling bad isn't the same as doing wrong." Then she messaged Priti for him anyway.

qa.q: How many times had Noor covered for Eshaan after March?
qa.a: She covered for him twice after that.

qa.q: What was Noor likely feeling when Eshaan made his request?
qa.a: Noor probably felt a bit guilty, as she later admitted, but calm enough to check the facts before answering.

qa.q: How did Noor separate real guilt from pressure?
qa.a: She checked the roster to see if she owed him, found she didn't, kept her decision, and still showed care by messaging Priti for him.

qa.q: How did Eshaan react to Noor's answer?
qa.a: Eshaan seemed annoyed, rolling his eyes, because his guilt-trip did not work.

grounding: A colleague observes an adult checking whether she actually owed a coworker, keeping her decision, and still showing care.

passage:
Sunday: Urmila told Farhan she wouldn't run the weekend chaat stall with him next season; her new job had Saturday shifts. Farhan stared at the tawa. "After I taught you everything. Fine. I'll manage. Somehow." Urmila went home with her stomach in knots and almost texted, "Forget it, I'll do it."
Tuesday: At the bus stop she made two columns in her notes. Did I break a promise? No, they had agreed on one season. Did I hurt him by lying or being careless? No. Is he sad? Yes. Is that the same as me doing wrong? She sat with that until her bus came.
Friday: She met him at the stall before opening. "I'm grateful you taught me, and I'll miss this. My answer is still no. My cousin Irfan wants weekend work; can I send him over?" Farhan was quiet, then nodded. Urmila walked away sad, but not guilty.

qa.q: What did Urmila's new job have that clashed with the stall?
qa.a: Her new job had Saturday shifts.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel after Farhan's reply on Sunday?
qa.a: Urmila felt guilty, with her stomach in knots, so pressured that she almost texted to take the stall back.

qa.q: How did Urmila's two columns help her decide?
qa.a: They separated real wrongs, such as breaking a promise, from Farhan's sadness, so she could keep her decision while still showing care in words.

qa.q: What might Farhan feel when Urmila offers her cousin Irfan?
qa.a: Farhan may still feel disappointed, but the thanks and the offer show care, which may ease his hurt and explain his nod.

grounding: Shows a person checking whether they actually wronged someone, then keeping the decision while showing care, because compassion is not compliance.
